absent: Register programming and timing inside the INIT sequence primitive
Layout and lifetime of trampoline headers, initial control and stack variables
Selection and behavior of APIC driver wakeup methods and platform legacy flags
Per-CPU interrupt stack allocation and firmware reset vector mechanics
Unwinder internals and entry register extraction
Text patching primitive and cross-CPU synchronization guarantees
Scheduler topology, self test and cache initialization work
Memory type save, vector protection, interrupt migration and LAPIC offline mechanics
Range validation and fault control primitives for user memory access
Native file and memory helpers behind the compatibility wrappers

findings.text: Secondary wakeup routine takes a physical APIC target, a start address and a logical CPU number, issues INIT signalling followed by conditional STARTUP signalling, and returns a combined delivery status.

Per-CPU bringup prepares current task state, stack guard and interrupt stacks, while the kick path validates the APIC target, saves memory type state, clears floating point ownership, then drives common preparation and boot.

Boot driver selects a default or 64-bit trampoline address, points initial control at secondary entry, configures per-CPU stack or control state, announces the CPU, optionally arms a legacy reset vector, then prefers 64-bit wakeup, then legacy wakeup, then INIT wakeup, cleaning the vector on failure.

Offline path recomputes threading limits, detaches sibling and cache sharing state, removes the CPU from online and NUMA membership, disables floating point use, migrates interrupts, takes the local APIC offline, then parks the CPU in a halt or idle loop.
Alternate build without hotplug support reports unimplemented disable and halts unconditionally in the park routine.

Boot coordination covers boot-CPU preparation, SMP disable during early init, parallel bringup enablement, completion handling with topology and self test finalization, and resume handling that defers then completes cache initialization.
Stack tracing offers a best-effort walker, a reliable walker that can fail, and a user-space walker, all delivering instruction addresses to a caller supplied consumer.

Static call support validates existing instruction bytes, derives a target operation from null and tail attributes, patches trampoline or inline sites, and provides an early boot patch primitive for trampolines.

Single-step helpers linearize the current instruction pointer across virtual modes, detect trap-flag altering instructions, arm single-step and system call exit traps, and expose separate user controls for single-step and block-step.
Compatibility wrappers adapt 32-bit truncate, file truncate, positioned read and write, advisory hints and readahead to native 64-bit offset and length forms.
Number of STARTUP signals is two when the boot CPU has an integrated APIC and zero otherwise.

Each STARTUP attempt clears and samples error state around the send when the local APIC version is large, waits for send completion, applies short or long pauses depending on a configurable delay selector, masks sampled errors, and stops early on send or accept failure while reporting delivery problems.

Boot uses a default trampoline address but switches to a 64-bit trampoline when that wakeup method exists, derives the secondary stack from the idle task register area, and on 32-bit builds programs descriptor and stack fields while on other builds it records the target CPU in a control word unless parallel mode is active.
Legacy warm reset vector setup and error clearing occur only when the platform advertises legacy reset support, and failure of any wakeup method triggers vector cleanup.
Kick aborts with an invalid argument status when the APIC identifier is marked bad, fails validity checks, or is absent from the present map.

Offline removal clears the departing CPU from core, die, sibling and shared cache membership of its peers, decrements per-core boot counts when the last thread leaves, clears active threading flags when a peer becomes solitary, resets local topology state, and refreshes the global threading maximum from remaining online CPUs.

Disable first detaches topology, forbids kernel floating point, removes online and NUMA membership under vector protection, migrates interrupts, takes the local unit offline, and only then soft disables the local APIC so already pending events remain visible while later arrivals may be lost.

Reliable walk succeeds for user tasks reaching user mode, fails when kernel mode registers appear on a frame-pointer build, fails on missing return addresses or consumer refusal, and fails when the unwinder reports corruption.

User walk starts from the frame pointer and instruction pointer, validates each user frame, and stops when validation fails, when the frame lies below the stack pointer, when the return address is zero, or when the consumer declines further entries.

Validation requires a fixed trailing marker on trampolines, accepts jump, return or conditional jump encodings for tail sites, and accepts call, multi-byte no-operation, zeroing, warning, and optionally unlock sequences for non-tail sites, halting on any other encoding.
Target operation is computed arithmetically from tail and null attributes so the four combinations map to distinct call, placeholder, jump and return behaviors in increasing order.
Early trampoline update is permitted only while the system is still booting and before static call initialization completes, writes a direct jump, and synchronizes the instruction stream.

Trap-flag analysis reads up to fifteen bytes at the linearized address and skips size, segment, lock, repeat and 64-bit extension prefixes, reporting true only for pop flags and interrupt return opcodes while treating other first significant bytes as negative.

Enabling single-step restores a pending trap flag, sets single-step and system call exit trap state, sets the trap flag, clears forced marking when the next instruction can change the flag itself, preserves prior user trap state, and reports whether block stepping may proceed.
Each compatibility wrapper forms native 64-bit positions or lengths by shifting the high half by thirty two bits and combining it with the low half before delegating to the native helper.

Announcement caches field widths, groups CPUs by node with headers during early boot while padding the bootstrap entry, and switches to one line per CPU with node, processor and APIC details once running.

Parallel bringup is refused when the platform disables it, otherwise it arms a mode that reads APIC identifiers at startup; resume defers cache initialization at begin and completes it at end; completion finalizes topology, self test, friendship and cache state.

Linearization returns a segment shifted address for virtual 8086 mode, adds local descriptor base for local selectors with sixteen bit masking when needed, and yields an all-ones result for missing tables or out of range selectors.
Secondary wakeup disables preemption across INIT sequencing, STARTUP loop and status collection, re-enabling only before returning.
Offline map removal holds the vector lock while clearing online and NUMA membership, with interrupt migration and APIC offline handling outside that hold but in a fixed order.
Static call site mutation holds the text mutex across validation and patching of trampoline and inline locations.
Local descriptor inspection holds the target address space context lock while checking table presence and bounds and reading the entry base.
User frame copying disables page faults only around the two user reads and re-enables immediately after, following an explicit access range check.
User stack frame layout holds a user-space pointer to the next frame followed by a return address word.

Secondary bringup progresses from INIT broadcast through zero or two timed STARTUP attempts with per-attempt send and accept evaluation to success only when both statuses are clear, otherwise failure with cleanup.

CPU offline progresses from topology detach through floating point revocation and map removal to interrupt migration, local APIC offline, soft disable, and finally a non-returning park through firmware shutdown and idle handling into halt.

Debug stepping moves from single-step arming to trap flag set, then either forced marking for ordinary instructions or unforced passthrough for flag-changing instructions, with block stepping enabled only when single-step reports permission and disabled otherwise.
Halt and park routines are non-returning CPU idle entries that flush caches on newer processors and loop in halt after optional speculation, firmware and idle transitions.
User stepping controls and stack walkers serve as debugger and tracer entries operating on a target task and register snapshot with a consumer callback.
Hotplug glue entries delegate preparation, kick, cleanup and synchronization to a platform operations table, with direct fallbacks for logging and polling when hooks are absent.
Failed delivery or acceptance is only reported through logs while the combined status propagates to the caller, so callers must treat any nonzero result as wakeup failure and restore reset state.
Interrupts arriving after local APIC soft disable do not set pending state and are invisible to migration, so disable must follow interrupt fixup to avoid silent loss.
Unexpected static call bytes or a mismatched trampoline marker halt the system, treating text corruption as fatal rather than recoverable.
User stack traversal trusts user frame pointers only after range validation and fault-protected reads, and must stop on backward or zero progress to avoid loops or faults.
Linearization of local selectors without proper locking or bounds checks could race table teardown or read out of range entries, hence the context lock and all-ones fallback are required.
Instruction selector enumeration orders five members starting at zero as call site, conditional call placeholder, jump, return, and conditional jump.
Trampoline guard occupies three bytes with values 0x0f, 0xb9 and 0xcc in order.
Five byte zeroing placeholder holds values 0x2e, 0x2e, 0x2e, 0x31 and 0xc0 in order.
Five byte return placeholder starts with the architectural return opcode followed by four fill bytes.
Five byte warning placeholder holds values 0x67, 0x48, 0x0f, 0xb9 and 0x3a in order.
Two five byte unlock patterns share leading values 0x3e, 0x3e and 0xc6, diverge in the fourth byte with 0x07 versus 0x00, and both terminate with 0x00.
Compatibility address helper converts its argument to an unsigned long before combining high and low halves.
